title: First Brunswick recording with Freddy Johnson, June 1933
summary: Warming up in a studio at 9 a.m., Briggs and Johnson improvised 'Grabb'n Blues' and then 'Japanese Sandman' unrehearsed, which Canetti recorded.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well, okay, so now, -- we're jumping around here a little bit, but that's all right.
Okay, now the Hot Club it all started, and this was all going now.
Yes.
I want to sort of move along to when you started recording then again, with your band, the Harlemites --
Yes, yes, well, we're about there now.
Briggs
Right.
As I explained, we -- the band was just an augmentation of -- we just augmented Bricktop's band, that we had at Bricktop's, and we were given a chance by Mr. Jacques Canetti, to record for Brunswick.
So, as we -- we would have -- I told you that the form that I gave you, the formation -- did we mention names, at all?
Yes, we have that down.

Well, it happened that our first recording was just one of those things, we went to a studio one morning, at 9:00 o'clock, after working until 4:00 or 5:00 o'clock in the morning, and I was in a corner, warming my instrument up, and so was Freddy.
Freddy was in another corner, playing his piano.
And, all of a sudden, Mr. Canetti who was in the tape room, he made us a sign,
Briggs

he made a sign, in other words, to say, "Keep on going." So we understood -- I don't know whether Freddy kept on -- we both kept on going, 'cause he was following it -- I was playing, and I was following everything he was doing. I was playing "Grabb'n Blues".
Right.

This is how I started. And we kept on. We kept going. And without saying a word to each other, as he was -- 'cause he was about almost -- you remember the recordings in those days, we were not close to each other. He was about two or three yards from where I was. And when I finished with the first chorus, I nodded to him and he took over. And, we continued until the end of it -- it was simple, you know, the end, 'cause, we did it together. I ended on a top F. I was just warming up. Both of us were just --
Briggs

And, after that number, Canetti came running down from the tape room, and he said, "My God, that's good." So we said, "What's good?" 'Cause we didn't know really, it was a take or nothing, 'cause we weren't prepared. We did nothing. We were just warming up. That's all.
And it seemed like everything I did for Freddy followed, and everything he did --
And then when he played the -- well, I said, "My God, is it possible." I was so happy, more than happy. So Canetti said, "Don't you have another number to go with just piano and trumpet?"

And Freddy said to me, "Why don't you try 'Japanese Sandman'," and I said, "Okay." He said -- I said, "Well, look, no rehearsal." I said, "We do it the same way," and that's what we did, and it came out.
Briggs
Great. This record that we've just been talking about, was recorded in about June of 1933 in Paris?
Sure.
That was a Brunswick record, but we don't have any further details on it than that.
(A recording of Arthur Briggs and Freddie Johnson is played at this time.)
But we want to get this in at the end. How are we going to do it?
